778.title: Where is thy sting?
778.hook: Paul: O death, where is thy sting? (1 Corinthians 15:55)
778.howItsDone: Some churches read 1 Corinthians 15 at funerals and at Easter, and the words "O death, where is thy sting?" are read aloud or sung in services about the resurrection.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Martha on the road and the words the resurrection and the life. Your line was christians hope this. Did Martha come to mind? Today, the same hope, shouted at death itself. Day seven hundred seventy-eight.

A letter is being read aloud to the church in Corinth. The writer is Paul, and he has heard something troubling. Some in the community have been saying there's no rising from the dead at all. His question to them is blunt: "how say some among you that there is no resurrection of the dead?" What follows is a long, careful argument. Then, near the end, the argument stops sounding like an argument. Paul turns away from the people in the room and speaks straight to death, the way you'd speak to a bully who has finally been cornered.
screen: `A LETTER TO CORINTH.` → `SOME SAY NO ONE RISES.` → `PAUL TURNS AND SPEAKS TO DEATH.`

segments.voice: First, an enemy. Paul doesn't pretend death is gentle or natural or fine. He calls it by its name: "The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death." Whatever comfort comes next, it doesn't start by shrinking the loss. Second, a seed. To explain how the dead could rise, Paul reaches for a farmer's picture: "that which thou sowest is not quickened, except it die." A seed goes into the ground and what comes up looks nothing like the seed. "It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption." The body that rises, in Paul's telling, is changed, not just restarted. Third, the taunt. Paul says that when this change comes, "then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory." Some readers trace that saying to the prophets Isaiah and Hosea. And then the two questions: "O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?" It's almost playful, a little mocking, the tone of someone sure of how the story ends. Fourth, what the sting is. Paul doesn't leave the image vague. "The sting of death is sin," he writes, and then, "thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ." For Christians, the line isn't a denial that people die or that grief hurts. Paul himself has just called death an enemy. It's a claim about who wins in the end. Read slowly, it has two halves: a sting, and a victory, both asked after as if they had gone missing.
screen: `DEATH IS CALLED AN ENEMY.` · `A SEED SOWN, A BODY RAISED.` · `SWALLOWED UP IN VICTORY.` · `THE STING, NAMED.` · then, large: `WHERE IS THY STING?`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to read one line slowly. Breathe in, and on the out-breath let these words go by in your head: O death. Breathe. Where is thy sting? Breathe. O grave. Breathe. Where is thy victory? Then stop, and just notice what happens, without deciding what it should be. Defiance, doubt, comfort, nothing at all, any of it is fine. If you pray, you can let Paul's thanks follow the questions. Then let the words go and rest in the breath. The bell holds the time.
Where is thy sting? Paul's taunt to death in his letter to the Corinthians, a Christian claim that death will not win in the end. Today's word.
Your line: where is thy sting. Today, read one sentence you care about slowly, a phrase per breath, and listen to what each piece says. Day seven hundred seventy-eight.

779.title: Sister Death
779.hook: Francis, near the end of his life, adds a verse to his Canticle of the Creatures praising Sister Death
779.howItsDone: Franciscans and other Christians sing or pray the Canticle of the Creatures, and in Franciscan communities the death of a brother or sister is sometimes spoken of as the coming of Sister Death.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul's taunt: O death, where is thy sting? Your line was where is thy sting. Which sentence did you read slowly? Paul called death an enemy. Today, a saint calls it family. Day seven hundred seventy-nine.

Brother Sun. Sister Moon and the stars. Brother Wind. Sister Water. Brother Fire. Mother Earth. These are the names in a song by Francis of Assisi, written in the everyday Italian of his region rather than in church Latin. It's called the Canticle of the Creatures, or the Canticle of the Sun, and it praises God for each of them, one at a time, as if the whole world were a household. Tradition says that near the end of his life, sick and nearly blind, Francis added one more name to the family.
screen: `BROTHER SUN, SISTER MOON.` → `A SONG OF THE WHOLE HOUSEHOLD.` → `ONE MORE NAME, NEAR THE END.`

segments.voice: First, a family. Francis doesn't praise the sun as a lamp or water as a resource. He gives each a place at the table. Sister Water is useful and humble and precious and pure. Brother Fire is beautiful and strong. Everything in the song is kin. Second, one more sister. The new verse praises God for our Sister Bodily Death, from whom no living person can escape. Read that slowly. Francis doesn't say death is pleasant, or optional, or not real. He says it is certain. And then he calls it sister, the same word he used for the moon. Third, not a shrug. The verse goes on, and it isn't sentimental. It warns: woe to those who die in mortal sin. And it calls blessed those whom death finds doing God's holy will, for the second death will do them no harm. Some readers hear in that phrase an echo of the book of Revelation. For Francis, a sister can still be serious. Fourth, the difference a name makes. An enemy is something you fight. A sister is someone who comes, whether you are ready or not, but who belongs to the household. Yesterday Paul called death the last enemy. Today Francis calls it sister. Both words come from Christian voices. Death is the same in both. What changes is where it sits: outside the door, or at the table. Sister death.
screen: `EVERY CREATURE IS KIN.` · `OUR SISTER BODILY DEATH.` · `SERIOUS, NOT SENTIMENTAL.` · `AN ENEMY, OR A SISTER.` · then, large: `SISTER DEATH.`

segments.voice: Settle and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind one ending in your life that has already happened: a school year, a job, a move, a friendship that ran its course, a habit you finally put down. Not a raw loss, if that's too much today. A finished thing. Look at what it made room for. Then, in your own words or just with attention, thank it. Thank the ending as if it had been a sister walking you to a door. If you pray, you can offer that thanks to God, as Francis did. The bell holds the time.
Sister Death: Francis of Assisi's name for bodily death in his Canticle of the Creatures, certain and unavoidable, and still counted as family. Today's word.
Your line: sister death. Today, when something ends, even something small like a day's work, give it a nod before you move on. Day seven hundred seventy-nine.

780.title: Dying well
780.hook: old Christian handbooks taught the art of dying well
780.howItsDone: Some Christians prepare for death with prayer, confession, anointing or last rites, and by talking with family and clergy; chaplains and hospice teams may help with what people call a good death.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Francis and his song, and the name sister death. Which ending did you thank? Francis met that sister on his own terms. Today, old books that tried to teach everyone how. Day seven hundred eighty.

Old woodcuts, in pairs. In the first, a man lies in bed, plainly near the end, and little devils crowd the room, whispering, holding up things to tempt him. In the next, an angel stands close with an answer, and the devils fall back. The pictures come from a kind of old Christian handbook, copied, printed and translated. Its Latin title is two words, ars moriendi, the art of dying. A whole book, written for ordinary people, about how to do the one thing nobody gets to do twice.
screen: `A MAN IN BED, NEAR THE END.` → `DEVILS, THEN AN ANGEL.` → `A HANDBOOK FOR DYING.`

segments.voice: First, an art. Calling it an art is the surprise. An art is something you learn, practice and get better at. The handbook treats a good death the same way: not as luck, but as something a person can prepare for while still well. Second, the temptations. The book imagines the deathbed as a last struggle. The dying person is tempted to doubt their faith, to despair over everything they've done wrong, to grow impatient with pain, to feel proud of their own goodness, and to cling to their money, their things, and their people. Third, the answers. For each temptation the book offers a counter, spoken in the pictures by an angel. Against despair, trust in mercy. Against impatience, patience. Against pride, humility. Against clinging, letting go. It isn't a list of rules so much as a set of turns the heart can make, even at the very end. Fourth, the people in the room. The handbook also speaks to whoever sits at the bedside: questions to gently ask, prayers to read aloud, an image of the cross held where the dying person can see it. Dying well, in these books, was not meant to be done alone. And the handbooks carry a quiet suggestion: don't wait for the deathbed. The turns can be practiced now, on a day when nothing is wrong. Dying well.
screen: `DYING AS AN ART YOU CAN LEARN.` · `TEMPTATIONS AT THE BEDSIDE.` · `AN ANSWER FOR EACH ONE.` · `NOT DONE ALONE.` · then, large: `DYING WELL.`

segments.voice: Sit easily, with something to write on nearby if you have it. Let the breath settle. Then ask yourself, gently, without forcing an answer: what would dying well mean to me? Maybe it's who is there. Maybe it's what has been said, or forgiven. Maybe it's simply not being afraid. Let one sentence form, and don't polish it. If nothing comes, that's an answer too. If you pray, you can hold the question before God. After the bell, write the sentence down. The bell holds the time.
Ars moriendi: Latin for the art of dying, the name of old Christian handbooks that taught people how to prepare for a good death. Today's word.
Your line: dying well. Today, keep your sentence somewhere you'll find it again, and notice one small way to practice it before evening. Day seven hundred eighty.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gloomy medieval obsession with death.
what it means: a practical handbook for a good death, for the dying and those beside them.
what a scholar hears: illustrated versions pair each deathbed temptation with an angel's answer.

781.title: All Souls' Day
781.hook: on 2 November, Catholics pray for the dead
781.howItsDone: On All Souls' Day Catholics attend Mass for the dead, write names in a parish book of remembrance, visit and tend graves, and light candles; Orthodox Christians keep their own days for praying for the dead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the old art of dying, and your line, dying well. Did you write your sentence down? Those handbooks were about the hour of death. Today, what the living do afterward. Day seven hundred eighty-one.

A Catholic church on the second of November. Near the door, in some parishes, there's a book open on a stand, and people stop on their way in to write in it. Not messages. Names. A mother. A brother. A friend from school. A baby who never came home from the hospital. Later, during Mass, those names are remembered and prayed for. Outside, in some towns, families are already at the cemetery with flowers and candles. The day has a long official name. The short one is All Souls' Day.
screen: `A BOOK OPEN BY THE DOOR.` → `NOT MESSAGES. NAMES.` → `CANDLES AT THE CEMETERY.`

segments.voice: First, all of them. The Church calendar calls it the Commemoration of All the Faithful Departed, and it comes right after All Saints' Day. All Saints honors the holy ones. All Souls prays for all the faithful departed, the ordinary dead, the ones people knew. Second, why pray for them. Catholics teach that some who die in God's friendship are still being made ready for heaven, a cleansing the Church calls purgatory, and that the prayers of the living can help them. The text Catholics point to comes from the second book of Maccabees, where Judas Maccabeus and his men pray for fallen soldiers: "It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from sins." Third, who says what. Orthodox Christians also pray for the dead, with their own days of remembrance through the year. Churches shaped by the Reformation generally don't teach purgatory, and their Bibles don't count Maccabees among the books of the Old Testament, though they remember the dead in their own services and prayers. Nobody here needs to settle that today. Fourth, by name. Whatever the theology, the center of the day is a list. In parish churches, the old prayer asks for eternal rest and perpetual light for the dead. A person is remembered not as a number in a cemetery but by the name someone once called across a kitchen. By name.
screen: `ALL THE FAITHFUL DEPARTED.` · `PRAYERS THAT HELP THE DEAD.` · `CHURCHES SEE IT DIFFERENTLY.` · `THE CENTER IS A LIST OF NAMES.` · then, large: `BY NAME.`

segments.voice: Sit quietly and let the breath settle. Bring to mind someone who has died. It can be family, a friend, a teacher, someone you only knew a little. Say their name, silently or aloud. Give the name one full breath. If another name comes, give that one a breath too. There's no right number. If no one you knew has died, choose a name you've read on a gravestone or a memorial. If you pray, you can use the old words asking eternal rest and perpetual light for them. The bell holds the time.
All Souls' Day: the day after All Saints' Day, when Catholics pray for all the faithful departed, and remember the dead by name. Today's word.
Your line: by name. Today, say one name of someone who has died to someone who knew them, or write it somewhere it will be seen. Day seven hundred eighty-one.

screen: `DAY 781 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: EVERY SOUL SHALL TASTE DEATH.`

782.title: Every soul shall taste death
782.hook: every soul will taste of death (Quran 3:185)
782.howItsDone: Muslims recite this verse in sermons and at funerals, and some families have it carved on gravestones; it is recalled when news of a death arrives, alongside the Quran's words that we belong to God and to Him we are returning (2:156).

segments.voice: Yesterday, All Souls' Day and a book of names by a church door. Your line was by name. Whose name did you say? Today the Christian voices give way to Muslim ones, and to a line about every soul. Day seven hundred eighty-two.

A short line in Arabic. Kullu nafsin dha'iqatul mawt. In Pickthall's old English translation of the Quran, it reads: "Every soul will taste of death." The line is short enough to carve on a stone or say at a graveside, and some Muslims do both. It sits in the third surah, the family of Imran, near a verse about being tested and holding on with patience. It doesn't argue. It doesn't comfort, at least not yet. It just says what is going to happen, to everyone.
screen: `A SHORT ARABIC LINE.` → `EVERY SOUL WILL TASTE OF DEATH.` → `IT SAYS WHAT WILL HAPPEN.`

segments.voice: First, every soul. The Arabic word kull means each, all, every one. There's no list of exceptions. Elsewhere the Quran tells the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, that no human before him was given life forever. Every soul includes the strong and the weak, the famous and the forgotten, the one reading the verse aloud. Second, taste. The Quran could have said every soul will die. Instead it uses a word from the mouth: to taste. Some readers notice what that suggests. A taste is something you go through. The one who tastes is still there afterward. Third, the very next sentence. The verse goes on: you will be paid in full on the Day of Resurrection, and whoever is kept from the Fire and brought into the Garden has truly won. For Muslims, death is not a wall at the end of the road. It's a door, and what lies past it is accounting and mercy. Fourth, the last line. The verse closes: "The life of this world is but comfort of illusion." In Muslim teaching this is not a claim that the world is worthless, since the Quran praises its good things too, but a warning not to mistake the borrowed for the lasting. And the same opening words, every soul will taste death, come back in other surahs too, and in surah twenty-nine they are followed at once by a return to God. Every soul.
screen: `NO SOUL IS LEFT OFF THE LIST.` · `DEATH IS TASTED.` · `THEN THE DAY OF RESURRECTION.` · `THE BORROWED, NOT THE LASTING.` · then, large: `EVERY SOUL.`

segments.voice: Sit with the line quietly. Let the breath settle, and then let the words come once, slowly: every soul will taste of death. Don't add anything to it. Then, on each out-breath, let the words every soul be enough. Every soul in this building. Every soul on this street. The people you love, and the people you've never met. And you. Not as fear, just as a fact, held gently. If you pray, you can let the line sit inside your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Every soul shall taste death: the Quran's short line saying no one is left out: death is tasted, and then comes the Day of Resurrection. Today's word.
screen: `EVERY SOUL SHALL TASTE DEATH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: every soul. Today, when someone annoys you in a line or in traffic, say quietly: every soul. Then see if anything softens. Day seven hundred eighty-two.

783.title: An atom's weight
783.hook: whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it (Quran 99:7–8)
783.howItsDone: Surah az-Zalzalah is short, and some Muslims recite it in daily prayer; Muslims recall its last two verses as a reason not to belittle small good deeds or small wrongs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a short line from the Quran: every soul will taste of death. Your line was every soul. Did you say it to anyone in traffic? That verse pointed past death to a day of accounting. Today, how small the accounting gets. Day seven hundred eighty-three.

The ground moves. That's how the ninety-ninth surah of the Quran begins, the one called the Earthquake. The earth is shaken, and it throws up what it has been carrying. A person looks at it and asks: what is the matter with her? And on that day, the surah says, the earth tells her news. Then people come out in scattered groups to be shown what they did. And the surah ends with two lines so short and so balanced they're easy to carry: whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of ill will see it.
screen: `THE GROUND MOVES.` → `THE EARTH TELLS ITS NEWS.` → `PEOPLE ARE SHOWN WHAT THEY DID.`

segments.voice: First, the earth speaks. In this surah, the ground itself is a witness. The floor you walked on, the street you crossed, has been listening, and on that day it tells what happened on it. It's a strange and striking picture: nothing done anywhere goes unrecorded. Second, an atom's weight. Pickthall's translation reads: "And whoso doeth good an atom's weight will see it then, And whoso doeth ill an atom's weight will see it then." The Arabic phrase is mithqala dharratin, the weight of a dharra, something tiny. Pickthall chose atom. Some readers picture a small ant, or a speck of dust floating in a sunbeam. Either way, it's the smallest thing you can still name. Third, both directions. The two verses mirror each other. Small harms count: the sharp word, the little lie. But small goods count just as surely: the held door, the returned text. For Muslims, nothing is too small to be seen by God. Fourth, don't belittle it. In a hadith in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, tells a companion not to look down on any good deed, even meeting your brother with a cheerful face. Put next to this surah, the point is easy to hear. The great question of death, judgment and what comes after is answered here in the smallest unit there is. Not a grand gesture. An atom's weight, done today, on ground that remembers.
screen: `THE GROUND IS A WITNESS.` · `THE WEIGHT OF SOMETHING TINY.` · `SMALL GOOD AND SMALL ILL BOTH COUNT.` · `DON'T BELITTLE A KIND FACE.` · then, large: `AN ATOM'S WEIGHT.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath settle. Then let your mind go over the next few hours. Somewhere in them there's a small good waiting, so small it would be easy to skip: a message to someone who's alone, a dish washed that isn't yours, a cheerful face for a tired cashier. Pick one. Just one, and keep it small. Picture yourself doing it, and let the breath stay easy. If you pray, you can offer the small deed to God before you do it. After the bell, go and do it. The bell holds the time.
An atom's weight: the Quran's picture of the smallest deed, good or ill, which every person will see on the day of accounting. Today's word.
Your line: an atom's weight. Today, do the one small good you chose, and don't tell anyone about it. Day seven hundred eighty-three.

784.title: The eyes weep
784.hook: when his small son Ibrahim died, the Prophet wept: the eyes shed tears and the heart grieves (Sahih al-Bukhari)
784.howItsDone: Muslims point to this hadith to show that weeping over the dead is permitted and merciful, while wailing and words of protest against God's decree are discouraged; mourners are encouraged to say the Quran's words that we belong to God and to Him we are returning (2:156).

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ground that remembers and your line, an atom's weight. Which small good did you do? The week's last day brings tears, and a father holding his son. Day seven hundred eighty-four.

The house of a blacksmith named Abu Saif. His wife is nursing a little boy named Ibrahim, the son of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. A companion named Anas remembers going there with the Prophet, who took the child, kissed him and breathed in his smell, the way parents do. Some time later they came again. This time Ibrahim was dying. And Anas remembers what happened next: the Prophet's eyes began to fill with tears.
screen: `A BLACKSMITH'S HOUSE.` → `A FATHER KISSES HIS SON.` → `THE SECOND VISIT.`

segments.voice: First, a small son. The report in Sahih al-Bukhari doesn't start with doctrine. It starts with a father holding a child close enough to breathe him in. Before anything is said about death, we're shown love. Second, even you? A companion named Abdur Rahman ibn Awf is standing there, and he's surprised. He says something like: you too, O Messenger of God? As if a prophet should be above tears. Third, this is mercy. The Prophet answers him: this is mercy. The tears aren't a lapse in faith. In this report they are a sign of the mercy God puts in human hearts. Fourth, eyes, heart and tongue. Then the Prophet says the line the story is remembered for: the eyes shed tears and the heart grieves, and we say only what pleases our Lord. And then, to the child: O Ibrahim, we are saddened by your parting. Three parts of a person, each given its job. The eyes are allowed to weep. The heart is allowed to grieve. The tongue is asked to hold to what pleases God, no cursing fate, no wild words. For Muslims, patience in grief limits what is said, not whether tears fall. Look back over the week. Paul taunting death. Francis calling it sister. The old art of dying well. Names in a book on All Souls' Day. Every soul tasting death, an atom's weight of good. And now a father crying over his boy, and calling it mercy. The eyes weep.
screen: `A FATHER HOLDS HIS SON.` · `"EVEN YOU?"` · `TEARS ARE MERCY.` · `EYES WEEP, HEART GRIEVES, TONGUE HOLDS.` · then, large: `THE EYES WEEP.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath slow down. Bring to mind a loss, recent or old, large or small. You don't need to go looking for pain; just let whatever is near come close. If tears come, let them come. Nobody needs to see them, and there's nothing to fix. If they don't come, that's fine too. Just let the heart feel what it feels, and keep the words gentle, even the ones in your own head. If you pray, you can bring the grief to God as it is. The bell holds the time.
